title: Amalakwang (Ugandan roselle leaves with groundnut paste)

ingredients.name: roselle (malakwang) leaves, or sorrel; substitute baby spinach with the juice of 1 lemon
natural peanut butter or ground roasted groundnuts

steps: Wash the leaves and chop roughly.
Cook the onion in the oil for 4 minutes, then add the tomato and cook until soft.
Add the leaves and water, cover, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until wilted and tender.
Stir the peanut butter into a ladle of the cooking liquid until smooth, then pour it into the pot.
Simmer for 5 minutes, season, and add lemon juice if using spinach.
Serve with sweet potatoes, posho or rice.

title: Dek Agira (Ugandan Lango smooth mashed pigeon peas with peanut paste)

ingredients.name: dried pigeon peas or cooked beans
natural peanut butter or ground roasted groundnuts

steps: Soak the pigeon peas overnight, drain, then boil in the fresh water for 1 to 1.5 hours until soft enough to crush between your fingers.
Drain, saving some of the liquid. Mash the peas thoroughly until completely smooth and creamy, or blend them.
Return to a pot over low heat and stir in the peanut butter, a spoon of the oil, and salt.
Loosen with a little of the saved liquid until you have a thick, spoonable cream.
Drizzle with the remaining oil on top and serve warm with millet or cassava bread, sweet potatoes or boiled bananas.

title: Dek Ngor (Ugandan Acholi pigeon pea sauce)

ingredients.name: dried pigeon peas, or yellow split peas
vegetable oil, or shea butter if available
bicarbonate of soda (to soften the peas)

steps: Rinse the peas and soak them for 6 hours or overnight in plenty of water.
Drain and boil in the fresh water with the bicarbonate of soda for 1 to 1.5 hours until completely soft and starting to break up.
Mash roughly with a wooden spoon, or blend partly, leaving some texture.
In a separate pan, soften the onion in the oil for 5 minutes, add the tomatoes, and cook until they collapse.
Stir the tomato mixture into the peas, add salt, and simmer for 10 minutes until thick.
Serve with millet bread, cassava, sweet potatoes or posho.

title: Firinda (Ugandan mashed bean sauce)

ingredients.name: dried red or brown beans, soaked overnight

steps: Drain the soaked beans, put them in a pot with the water and boil for 1 hour or until very soft.
Drain, keeping a cup of the cooking liquid, and mash the beans with a masher, or push them through a sieve, until smooth.
In a pan, heat the oil and cook the onion for 5 minutes, then add the tomato and chilli for 3 minutes more.
Stir in the mashed beans and a few spoons of the reserved liquid, season with salt, and cook gently for 10 minutes, adding liquid until the sauce is thick but pourable.
Serve with matoke, sweet potatoes, millet bread or rice.

title: Katogo (Ugandan matoke and beef breakfast stew)

ingredients.name: matoke or green plantains, peeled and cut in chunks

steps: Cook the beef in the water with half the onion and a little salt for 30 to 40 minutes until almost tender.
Heat the oil in a wide pot and fry the rest of the onion and the garlic for 3 minutes, then add the tomatoes, pepper, carrot and curry powder.
Cook for 5 minutes until saucy, then add the beef with its stock.
Add the banana chunks, cover, and simmer for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the bananas are tender and have soaked up the sauce.
Adjust the salt and serve in bowls while hot.

title: Kikomando (Ugandan chapati cut and served with beans)

ingredients.name: cooked kidney beans or red beans

steps: Heat the oil and fry the onion and garlic until soft, about 5 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, cumin and salt and cook for 5 minutes until jammy.
Stir in the beans and the cooking liquid and simmer for 10 minutes, mashing a few beans to thicken.
Warm the chapatis in a dry pan, then tear or cut them into bite-size strips.
Put the chapati pieces on plates and spoon the hot beans over; toss lightly and serve.

title: Lakotokoto (Ugandan Acholi sesame sauce with beef)

ingredients.name: raw sesame seeds (simsim), or 6 tbsp tahini as a substitute

steps: Simmer the beef in the water with half the onion and a little salt for 30 minutes until tender.
Wash and grind the sesame seeds with a few spoons of water to a thick paste; if using tahini, just whisk with a little water.
In another pan, fry the remaining onion in the oil, then add the tomatoes until they break down.
Add the beef with its stock, then stir in the sesame paste a little at a time.
Cook gently for 15 minutes, stirring constantly so the sesame does not stick, until thick and the oil begins to separate.
Serve with millet bread, cassava or boiled sweet potatoes.

title: Matoke (Ugandan steamed green banana mash)

ingredients.name: matoke (green cooking bananas) or green plantains
banana leaf or foil, for wrapping (optional)

steps: Peel the bananas under running water or rub oil on your hands, as the sap stains; cut the flesh into chunks.
Sauté the onion in the oil for 3 minutes, add the tomato and cook until soft, then add the banana chunks, water and salt.
Tie everything into a banana-leaf parcel if you have one, or just cover the pot tightly. Cook over low heat for 35 to 45 minutes until very tender.
Drain off any excess liquid, then mash the bananas in the pot with a masher or the back of a wooden spoon until soft and cohesive.
Serve hot, in a mound, with a groundnut sauce, beans or a meat stew.

title: Mugoyo (Ugandan sweet potatoes mashed with beans)
steps: Boil the sweet potatoes in salted water for 15 to 20 minutes until tender.
Meanwhile, soften the onion in the oil for 5 minutes, then add the beans and a little liquid and warm through.
Drain the sweet potatoes and mash roughly in the pot.
Fold in the beans and onion, mixing well until the two are mingled but still textured.
Add liquid to adjust the consistency, season, and serve hot.

title: Sombe (Ugandan cassava leaf stew with groundnut paste)

ingredients.name: cassava leaves, frozen and thawed (or collard greens or spinach)

steps: Simmer the beef in the water with half the onion, the garlic and salt for 40 minutes until nearly tender.
Cassava leaves must be cooked thoroughly. Boil frozen or fresh cassava leaves in plenty of water for at least 30 minutes, then drain well; collards or spinach only need a quick blanch.
Fry the remaining onion in the oil, add the leaves and stir for 5 minutes.
Add the leaves to the beef with its stock and simmer, covered, for 25 minutes.
Mix the peanut butter with a ladle of the hot stock until smooth, stir into the pot, and cook for 10 minutes more.
Serve with posho, matoke, cassava or rice.
